sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know the formal prepositional phrase *mediante* ("by means of") from B1 Unit 24: *Mediante este sistema, se reduce el consumo de energía*. A noun follows it directly. In political history it is useful to say how something was done: by a vote, by a strike, by a law.

sections.title: Mediante + noun
rows: Los militares quisieron aprobar una Constitución mediante un plebiscito.
*mediante* + noun: by means of a plebiscite
Los uruguayos expresaron su rechazo mediante el voto.
En 1984 volvió el gobierno civil mediante elecciones.
El gobierno militar controlaba la información mediante la censura.

items.spanish: Los militares quisieron aprobar una Constitución mediante un plebiscito.
items.english: The military wanted to approve a constitution by means of a plebiscite.

items.spanish: Los uruguayos expresaron su rechazo mediante el voto.
items.english: Uruguayans expressed their rejection by voting.

items.spanish: En 1984 volvió el gobierno civil mediante elecciones.
items.english: In 1984 civilian government returned by means of elections.

items.spanish: El gobierno militar controlaba la información mediante la censura.
items.english: The military government controlled information by means of censorship.

sections.content: *Mediante* is followed by a noun, never by *de* (*mediante de*) or by a verb. It is formal: in everyday Spanish you say *con* or *por* (*con el voto*). It often opens the sentence, followed by a comma: *Mediante el voto, los uruguayos…*.
